Main article: [Bronx High School of Science](/wiki/Bronx_High_School_of_Science "Bronx High School of Science")

Bronx High School of Science was founded in 1938 as a specialized science and math high school for boys, by resolution of the [Board of Education of the City of New York](/wiki/Board_of_Education_of_the_City_of_New_York "Board of Education of the City of New York"), with [Morris Meister](/wiki/Morris_Meister "Morris Meister") as the first principal of the school. They were given use of an antiquated Gothic-gargoyled edifice located at Creston Avenue and 184th Street. The building, built in 1918 for Evander Childs High School, had been successively occupied by [Walton High School](/wiki/Walton_High_School_(New_York_City) "Walton High School (New York City)") (1930) and by an annex of [DeWitt Clinton High School](/wiki/DeWitt_Clinton_High_School "DeWitt Clinton High School") (1935). The initial faculty was comprised in part by a contingent from [Stuyvesant High School](/wiki/Stuyvesant_High_School "Stuyvesant High School").[[2]](#cite_note-StuyLandmark-2) Principal Meister put his imprint on the school from its formation, for example, selecting as school colors "green to represent chlorophyll and gold the sun, both of which are essential to the chain of life."[[3]](#cite_note-3)

The [cult image](/wiki/Cult_image "Cult image") of Athena Polias, which was bathed in the sea and to which was presented the *[peplos](/wiki/Peplos "Peplos")*, was an olive-wood *[xoanon](/wiki/Xoanon "Xoanon")*, located in another temple on the northern side of the Acropolis, more closely associated with the Great Altar of Athena.[[31]](#cite_note-Burkert-143-31) The [High Priestess of Athena Polias](/wiki/High_Priestess_of_Athena_Polias "High Priestess of Athena Polias") supervised the city cult of Athena based in the [Acropolis](/wiki/Acropolis "Acropolis"), and was the chief of the lesser officials, such as the [plyntrides](/wiki/Plyntrides "Plyntrides"), [arrephoroi](/wiki/Arrephoroi "Arrephoroi") and [kanephoroi](/wiki/Kanephoroi "Kanephoroi").[[32]](#cite_note-32)

The colossal statue of Athena by [Phidias](/wiki/Phidias "Phidias") was not specifically related to any cult attested by ancient authors[[33]](#cite_note-33) and is not known to have inspired any religious fervour.[[31]](#cite_note-Burkert-143-31) Preserved ancient sources do not associate it with any priestess, altar or cult name.[[34]](#cite_note-Nagy-55-34)
